title: Earthen Vessels
subtitle: Why Our Bodies Matter to Our Faith
blurb: The church inherited a lie it never examined: that the soul is the real you and the body is the cage you carry it in. This book argues the opposite from the center of the faith — that God made matter, entered it, died in it, rose in it, and intends to redeem it. Your body is not the obstacle to your discipleship. It is the place your discipleship happens or does not happen at all.

chapters.title: The Lie We Were Handed
chapters.summary: The dualism that splits spirit from body is not Christian. It is Greek, and the church absorbed it without noticing, teaching generations to despise the one thing God called good.
chapters.body:
I came to faith out of atheism, and I want to tell you what I expected to find when I crossed over. I expected to find a religion of escape. I expected the message to be that the world is a shadow, the body is a burden, and the point of all this praying and singing is to get out — to shed the flesh like a wet coat and float free into something purer. That is what the outside assumes Christianity is. A long preparation for leaving.

What surprised me was how wrong that was. And what grieved me, later, was how many believers think it is right.

The lie is old. It did not come from Genesis. It came from Athens. The Greek philosophical inheritance — Plato most of all — taught that the material world is a lower order of being, a dim copy of the real, and that the soul is a divine spark trapped in the prison of the body. The word they used for body, *soma*, rhymed in their minds with *sema*, a tomb. The body is the grave of the soul. Salvation, in that scheme, is the soul's escape from matter into pure mind, pure spirit, pure light.

The church grew up in a world soaked in that idea. And it absorbed it — not in the creeds, which fought it, but in the bloodstream of ordinary piety. We started saying things the Bible never says. We started singing about this world not being our home, about flying away. We started treating the body as the seat of sin and the spirit as the seat of holiness, as though lust lived in the flesh and prayer lived somewhere cleaner. We built a whole spirituality on the assumption that the more bodily a thing is, the less holy it must be.

It is not Christian. It is Gnostic. And the church spent its first three centuries fighting it for its life.

Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon in the second century, wrote five books against the Gnostics for one reason: they were telling Christians that the God of creation was a lesser, fumbling deity, and that the true God had nothing to do with mud and blood and birth. Irenaeus saw what was at stake. If matter is not God's, then the incarnation is a lie, the resurrection is a lie, and the bread on the table is just bread. He answered with a sentence the church should have tattooed on its hands: *Gloria Dei vivens homo.* The glory of God is a living human being. Not an escaped soul. A living human — flesh, lungs, hunger, all of it — fully alive. That is what God is glorified by.

Open the first page of the Bible and you find the same thing. Seven times in Genesis 1 God looks at what he has made — light, water, land, animals, the bodies of the first man and woman — and pronounces it good. "And God saw that it was good" (Genesis 1:25). Then, after he makes humanity, the verdict escalates: "it was very good" (Genesis 1:31). The Hebrew word is *tov*. It is not a grudging approval. It is delight. The material creation is not a regrettable necessity God tolerated on the way to making souls. It is the thing he wanted. He made dirt and called it very good, and then he reached into the dirt and made a man out of it.

That detail matters more than we let it. "The LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature" (Genesis 2:7). You are not a soul that happens to be wearing a body. You are dust that God breathed into. Take away the dust and there is no you. Take away the breath and there is no you. A human being, in the Hebrew imagination, is not a ghost in a machine. It is animated clay. Embodied spirit. The two are not at war. They are one thing, and God made it on purpose.

So where did we go wrong? We went wrong the moment we found the body inconvenient and reached for a theology that let us despise it. Because the body is inconvenient. It gets sick. It ages. It wants things we cannot always give it. It is the site of our deepest temptations and our most humiliating limits. And the Greek lie offered us an exit: this part of you is not the real you. Push it down. Transcend it. The real you is elsewhere.

I have preached to people who believed this so deeply they could not grieve their own aging. They thought it was unspiritual to mind that the body fails. I have sat with people who could not understand why their faith did not lift them out of depression, because they had been taught that a chemical, bodily thing should yield to a spiritual remedy, and when it did not they assumed the failure was theirs. The lie does not stay abstract. It costs people their peace.

And I have lived enough of it myself to know I am not pointing from the outside. I have prayed as though prayer were the soul's escape from the day rather than the dust's address to its Maker. I have treated my own exhaustion as a moral failing instead of a creature's honest limit. I learned the lie too. We all drank from the same well.

Here is what the rest of this book wants to say. The center of the Christian faith is not the soul's escape from matter. It is the opposite. It is God taking on matter. "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14). The eternal Son did not become a feeling or an idea. He became a body — with a digestive system and a sleep schedule and feet that got dirty on the roads of Galilee. He was born the way you were born. He got tired the way you get tired. And when he rose from the dead, he did not rise as a spirit. He rose with a body the disciples could touch, a body that ate fish on a beach.

If that is true, then the body is not the cage. The body is the point.

I want to take you through the whole of it — health and limit, sex and hunger, work and rest, suffering and aging, death and the resurrection hope. Not as topics. As territory God claims. Every chapter is going to press the same conviction against a different part of your life: that the material world is not a distraction from your discipleship but the place it happens.

We were taught to hate the gift and call it holiness. It is time to repent of that.
chapters.verdict: We were taught to hate the gift and call it holiness.
reflect: Where did you first learn that your body was a problem to be managed rather than a gift to be received?
What would change in your prayers if you believed God cared about your knees, your appetite, your fatigue?
Whose voice still tells you that the spiritual is the opposite of the physical?

chapters.title: The Word Became Flesh
chapters.summary: The incarnation is not God visiting the body; it is God becoming one. The scandal of Christmas is that the infinite took on digestion, fatigue, and a death certificate.
chapters.body:
There is a sentence in the Gospel of John that the early church fought over for centuries, and most of us read it as though it were soft. "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory" (John 1:14). We hear it at Christmas, wrapped in candlelight, and it sounds gentle. It is not gentle. It is the most violent collision of categories ever written down.

The Word — *Logos*, the eternal reason and order of God, the one through whom all things were made — became *sarx*. Flesh. John could have used a cleaner word. Greek had words for body that carried less baggage. He chose the one that meant meat, mortality, weakness, the part of you that decays. The Logos became meat. The mind of God acquired a metabolism.

To the Greek world this was not merely strange. It was disgusting. A respectable Greek philosopher could believe in a divine principle ordering the cosmos. What he could not stomach was that this principle would lower itself into the indignity of a human body — into birth, with all its blood, into hunger, into the bowels and the bladder and the slow corruption of aging. The whole point of being divine was to be free of that. John says God chose it.

And he did not choose a halfway version. The Gnostics, when they could not avoid the incarnation entirely, tried to soften it. They said Jesus only seemed to have a body, that he was a phantom who left no footprints, that the divine Christ descended on the man Jesus at his baptism and abandoned him before the cross so that God would not have to suffer. The church had a word for this: docetism, from the Greek for "to seem." And the church rejected it absolutely, because it understood what was being protected and what was being lost. If Jesus only seemed to have a body, then God only seemed to save us.

The creeds got specific on purpose. He was "conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary." Born. Not appeared. Born the way you were born, through a woman's labor, into the smell of a stable. "Suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, dead, and buried." Dead. Not seemed to die. The creeds are stubbornly physical because the salvation depends on it being physical.

Consider what the Gospels are willing to tell you about this body. He was hungry — forty days into the wilderness, "he was hungry" (Matthew 4:2), and the tempter went straight for the bread because the body's need was real. He was thirsty — at a well in Samaria, "tired as he was from the journey," he asked a woman for a drink (John 4:6). He slept so deeply in a boat that a storm did not wake him. He wept at a grave. He was, the letter to the Hebrews insists, tempted in every way as we are, which means the pull of the body — toward comfort, toward safety, toward the easy road — was a pull he actually felt. There is no asterisk. The fatigue was real fatigue. The hunger was real hunger.

I think we resist this more than we admit. We carry a quiet docetism of our own. We imagine a Jesus who walked an inch off the ground, who never had a headache, who was never genuinely tired in his bones at the end of a day of need pressing in on him from every side. We picture a glow where there should be a face. And we do it for a reason that feels reverent: we want to protect God's dignity. But the gospel is precisely that God laid his dignity down. "Though he was in the form of God," Paul writes, he "emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men" (Philippians 2:6-7). He did not consider equality with God a thing to clutch. He took on flesh and the flesh's whole humiliating itinerary, all the way to a state execution.

Why does this matter for you, in your body, tonight?

Because it means there is no part of your bodily life that is beneath God or foreign to him. He knows hunger from the inside. He knows what it is to be so tired that words come slow. He knows the body's fear in the face of pain — in Gethsemane he sweat and shook and begged for another way. When you bring God your exhaustion, you are not bringing him a problem he finds distasteful. You are bringing him something he has felt. The eternal Son carries the memory of aching feet.

Athanasius, defending all this against the Arians in the fourth century, put the logic plainly: what is not assumed is not healed. If the Son did not take on a real human body, then real human bodies are not redeemed. He took on flesh so that flesh could be saved — not deleted, not escaped, but saved. The incarnation is not a rescue mission to extract souls from a sinking ship. It is God climbing down into the hold to be where the bodies are.

Eugene Peterson spent a career insisting that the gospel is relentlessly local and physical — that "the Word became flesh and moved into the neighborhood" is not decoration but the whole method. God does not save us by hovering. He saves us by inhabiting. He does his redeeming work in particular places, through particular bodies, in real time, in the dust.

I think of the years I spent as an atheist explaining away the resurrection, and how I never once stopped to be scandalized by the incarnation, because I did not understand it well enough to be offended. I thought Christianity was about the spirit escaping the world. The longer I have pastored, the more I have come to see it is the reverse, and the reverse is harder. Anyone can long to leave. It takes a God to come.

He did not rescue us from matter. He moved in. And he has not left.
chapters.verdict: God did not rescue us from matter. He moved in.
reflect: What parts of being human do you secretly think God would never lower himself to share?
How does it change your sense of your own ordinary body to know the Son of God had one exactly like it?
When you imagine Jesus, do you imagine a body or a glow?

chapters.title: Treasure in Jars of Clay
chapters.summary: Paul does not promise that the gospel will make our bodies strong. He locates the gospel's power precisely in their weakness, so the glory cannot be mistaken for ours.
chapters.body:
There is a verse people quote when they want to feel encouraged, and I want to slow it down, because Paul did not write it to encourage. He wrote it to redefine where strength comes from. "But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us" (2 Corinthians 4:7).

A jar of clay was the cheapest container in the ancient world. Pottery was disposable. You did not admire a clay jar; you used it until it cracked and then you threw the shards on the trash heap, where archaeologists dig them up by the millions today. That is the image Paul reaches for to describe the human body — including his own apostolic, miracle-working, gospel-preaching body. Cheap. Breakable. Bound for the trash heap. And inside it, the treasure of the knowledge of God.

Now read the reason he gives. The treasure is in clay *to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us.* The fragility is not an unfortunate side effect. It is the design. If God had put his gospel into bodies of bronze, into people who never got sick, never broke down, never aged or failed, then the world would look at those people and conclude the power was theirs. The strength of the container would steal the glory from the treasure. So God chose clay. He chose to carry the most valuable thing in the universe in the most breakable thing in the room, so that when the light shines out, no one can mistake whose light it is.

This cuts directly against a teaching that has poisoned a great deal of modern faith — the assumption that a healthy faith should produce a healthy body, that if you really believed, you would not be sick, that physical suffering is a sign of spiritual deficiency. It is a cruel doctrine, and it is the opposite of Paul. Read on in the same letter and you find a man cataloguing his beatings, his shipwrecks, his sleepless nights, his hunger. You find him pleading with God three times to remove a "thorn in the flesh," some bodily affliction he never names, and you find God refusing: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). Paul does not get the strong body. He gets a stronger word. The power is perfected — completed, brought to its full form — not in his health but in his weakness.

I have stood at too many bedsides to preach anything else. I have watched people of deep faith waste away from cancer. I have prayed for healings that did not come. And I have come to believe that the question "why didn't God make this body strong" is the wrong question, asked from inside the lie that strength is the point. The body was never going to be strong forever. Yours will not be. Mine will not be. Every jar of clay cracks. The only question is whether anything worth seeing was inside it when it did.

Listen again to the verses that follow, because Paul does not leave us with a tidy comfort. He gives us a rhythm. "We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed; always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies" (2 Corinthians 4:8-10). Carrying in the body the death of Jesus. The body is where the dying happens. And the body is where the life of Jesus becomes visible — not despite the dying, but through it. The crack is how the light gets out.

Brueggemann taught a generation of preachers that the Bible refuses to pretend. The psalms of lament — and there are more of them than there are psalms of praise — give the body's anguish full voice. "My strength fails because of my iniquity, and my bones waste away" (Psalm 31:10). The Bible does not tell the suffering body to be quiet and spiritual. It hands the suffering body a microphone. There is a faith that can only sing when the body is well. The faith of Scripture sings from the trash heap.

I want to name where this lands, because it is easy to keep abstract. Somewhere in your body right now there is a crack — a diagnosis, a limit, a chronic ache, a failing you would never volunteer in a prayer meeting because it feels like evidence against your faith. I want to tell you that Paul would have put it at the center of his testimony, not the edge. The thing you are ashamed of is the thing God means to shine through. Not because suffering is good. Suffering is an enemy, and we will get to that. But because the God who put treasure in clay knew exactly what clay does. He was not surprised by your fragility. He counted on it.

There is a self-implication I cannot avoid here. I have wanted to be a bronze jar. I have wanted to be the kind of pastor whose strength was its own argument, whose competence preached, whose unbroken life testified to a manageable God. And every time God has used me, it has been through the cracks — through the failures I could not hide, the limits I could not pray away, the days the need outran the strength. The light I have seen get out of me got out through the broken places. It humiliates me to write that. It is also the only true thing I know about ministry.

The cracks are not the failure of the plan. They are the plan.
chapters.verdict: The cracks are not the failure of the plan. They are the plan.
reflect: What weakness in your body are you most ashamed to bring before God?
Have you been taught that strong faith should produce a strong, untroubled body?
Where in your life is the light getting out only because something in you is broken open?

chapters.title: This Temple
chapters.summary: Paul calls the body a temple of the Spirit not to shame us into self-improvement but to declare that God has taken up residence in the flesh he made.
chapters.body:
There is a line in First Corinthians that gets pressed into service for everything from purity talks to fitness sermons, and almost always it gets read backwards. "Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body" (1 Corinthians 6:19-20).

We usually hear it as a command to take care of ourselves — eat right, do not abuse the equipment, treat the body like a sacred machine you are renting. That is not nothing, but it misses the staggering thing Paul is actually saying. He is not saying your body is *like* a temple. He is saying the Holy Spirit of the living God lives inside it. The same God whose presence filled Solomon's temple with a glory the priests could not stand up under — that God has chosen the human body as his dwelling. Not the soul, abstractly. The body. *In* you. The flesh you carry to work, the flesh that aches when you wake up, the flesh you are sometimes ashamed of — that is the sanctuary God moved into at Pentecost.

To understand the weight of this you have to understand what a temple was. In the ancient world a temple was the single point where heaven touched earth, where the divine presence was localized and accessible, where the gap between God and people was bridged. Israel's whole life oriented toward the temple in Jerusalem. To say the body is a temple is to say the body is now that meeting place. The bridge between heaven and earth runs through your skin.

This is why Paul brings it up in the context he does, which we politely skip over. The Corinthians had a slogan: "All things are lawful for me" (1 Corinthians 6:12). They used it to justify sleeping with prostitutes, on the theory — straight out of the Greek dualism we have been tracking — that the body does not matter to God, that what you do with your flesh is spiritually irrelevant because the flesh is just temporary packaging. Paul detonates the theory. "The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body" (1 Corinthians 6:13). The Lord *for the body.* God is committed to your flesh. He is not indifferent to it. He bought it.

That phrase — "you were bought with a price" — is the key that turns the whole lock. Paul's argument for honoring God in the body is not "your body is sacred so keep it clean." It is "your body belongs to God because God paid for it with the body of his Son." The price was a crucifixion. Christ did not redeem an abstract you. He redeemed the embodied you, every cell, with his own torn flesh. And what God paid that much for, he intends to keep. The body is not a holding cell for the soul until the real rescue. The body is part of what was rescued.

Here is the implication I find people most resist, including myself. There is no such thing as a spiritual life separate from your physical life. We keep two ledgers. In one we record prayer, Scripture, worship, the things we file under "spiritual." In the other we record what we eat, how we sleep, how we use our hands, what we look at, how we touch and are touched — the things we file under "just physical, just life." And we behave as though God audits only the first ledger. Paul collapses the two into one. If the Spirit dwells in your body, then what you do with your body is your spiritual life. There is no other one. The way you treat your flesh and the flesh of others is not a footnote to your discipleship. It is the text.

James K. A. Smith has spent years arguing that we are not primarily thinking things but desiring, embodied things — that we are shaped less by what we believe in our heads than by what we love with our bodies, by the habits and rhythms and physical practices that train our desires before we ever reason about them. He calls our daily routines liturgies, because they form us whether we notice or not. The coffee shop forms us. The phone in our hand forms us. The commute forms us. We become what our bodies repeatedly do. If that is true — and I am convinced it is — then the temple is being decorated every day, by every habit, for one god or another. The question is never whether your body is being formed. It is who is moving in.

I want to be careful here, because this teaching has been weaponized. Pastors have used "your body is a temple" to shame people about weight, to police women's clothing, to load fragile people with guilt about food and appearance until the word "temple" became a whip. That is a desecration of the verse. Paul is not handing you a standard to fail. He is announcing a residence. The shape of honoring God in your body is not a number on a scale. It is the offering of your actual flesh — its work, its rest, its sexuality, its limits — as a place where God is at home and visible.

I confess I have lived a divided life longer than I would like to admit. I have prayed well and lived in my body carelessly, as though God cared about my words and not my Tuesdays. I have treated rest as theft and my appetites as private and my fatigue as God's blind spot. The temple was never empty during those years. The Spirit was in the building the whole time, in rooms I had locked and labeled "not spiritual."

God does not haunt the body. He dwells in it. Act like the owner is home.
chapters.verdict: God does not haunt the body. He dwells in it.
reflect: Do you treat your body as something you own and use, or as a place God inhabits?
What would honoring God in your body look like this week, concretely?
Where have you split your "spiritual life" from your physical one as if they were separate accounts?

chapters.title: The Limits of the Creature
chapters.summary: Finitude is not the fall. To have a body is to have a limit, and the first temptation was the refusal to accept one.
chapters.body:
The serpent's first move in the garden was not to suggest a sin. It was to suggest a limit was an insult. "You will be like God" (Genesis 3:5). The whole seduction turns on the idea that being a creature — bounded, dependent, finite — is beneath us, and that the way up is to throw off the limit and become unbounded, self-sufficient, divine. The fall is not fundamentally about an apple. It is about the refusal to be a creature.

I say this because we have confused two things that the Bible keeps apart: finitude and fallenness. Finitude means you are limited — you have a body that can only be in one place, that needs sleep, that gets tired, that will die. Fallenness means you are sinful — your will is bent, your loves are disordered. We treat these as the same problem. We feel our limits as a kind of shame, as though needing rest or food or help were evidence that something has gone wrong with us. But the limits came before the fall. God built them into the design and called the design very good.

Look at the creation account again. On the seventh day God rests (Genesis 2:2-3). God does not rest because he is tired; God does not get tired. He rests to establish a rhythm, to write a limit into the architecture of the week itself, to declare that the world does not run on ceaseless production. And he makes humanity to live inside that rhythm — to sleep when it is dark, to stop when the week turns, to eat and be filled and need to eat again. The first humans were finite before they were fallen. They needed God, needed each other, needed the garden, needed sleep. That neediness was not the curse. It was the goodness.

The lie tells you that your limits are the problem to overcome. The technology of our age agrees with the lie. We have built a world that treats sleep as negotiable, presence as optional, availability as something that should be total. We carry devices that promise to make us everywhere at once, to free us from the body's stubborn here-and-now. And we feel, more than ever, the specific exhaustion of creatures pretending to be infinite. We are not tired because we have failed. We are tired because we were never meant to be God, and we keep trying.

Wendell Berry has written about this for decades from a farm in Kentucky, and the heart of his argument is that human beings are creatures, made to live within limits — the limits of a body, a place, a community, a span of years — and that nearly every modern catastrophe comes from the refusal to accept that we are not the Creator. He calls it the difference between the way of a creature and the arrogance of trying to be unlimited. A good life, he insists, is a life lived gratefully inside its proper bounds. The land has limits. The body has limits. Pretending otherwise does not transcend them; it ruins them.

The Psalms know this. "He knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust" (Psalm 103:14). That is not an accusation. It is tenderness. God remembers that you are dust — fragile, temporary, limited — and the remembering moves him to compassion, not contempt. "As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him" (Psalm 103:13). I grew up without a father, and I have spent my life turning over what that word means. Here it means a father who does not resent his child's smallness. Who does not demand that the child be more than a child. Who remembers the dust and is gentle with it.

We are not gentle with our own dust. We schedule as though we will not need to sleep. We say yes as though we could be in two places. We measure our worth by output, which means we measure our worth by the degree to which we have defeated our limits — and so every limit becomes a verdict against us. The tired body becomes proof of failure. The aging body becomes an enemy. The need for help becomes a humiliation. We have made a sin out of finitude, which means we have made a sin out of the way God made us.

I have done this in ministry more than I want to confess. A pastor is handed a job with no natural edges — there is always another visit, another sermon, another person in crisis at midnight — and the temptation is to behave as though the limits do not apply to you, as though needing rest were a lack of love, as though your body's demand for sleep were a spiritual weakness you could pray through. I have treated my own creatureliness as the obstacle to my usefulness. And I have watched it nearly cost me the things that matter, because a man who cannot accept that he is dust will eventually try to be a god to people, and that ends only one way.

The accepting of limits is not resignation. It is worship. Every time you go to sleep, you confess that the world will go on without you for eight hours, that you are not the one holding it together. Every time you stop work unfinished, you confess that the kingdom does not depend on your output. Every time you say "I cannot, I am only one person," you tell the truth about being a creature, and telling the truth is always closer to God than the lie ever was.

You were made to need. The Son of God himself needed sleep, needed food, needed friends, needed the Father. He did not apologize for it. Neither should you. Stop apologizing for it.
chapters.verdict: You were made to need. Stop apologizing for it.
reflect: Which of your creaturely limits do you treat as a defect rather than a design?
Where are you trying to be infinite — available, productive, unsleeping — as though limits were sin?
What would it mean to receive your finitude as a gift instead of fighting it as a flaw?

chapters.title: Hunger and the Table
chapters.summary: Eating is the most ordinary thing we do and one of the most theological, which is why God's people are commanded to feast, why the church gathers at a table, and why food disorders our worship when it disorders our desire.
chapters.body:
God could have made us so that we never needed to eat. He could have made bodies that ran on light or air or nothing at all. Instead he made us hungry — made us so that three times a day, every day, for the whole of our lives, the body sends up its insistent need and we have to stop and receive something from outside ourselves to go on living. Hunger is a daily lesson in dependence, built into the flesh. You cannot be self-sufficient and eat.

And God did not treat this need as a low animal function to be managed discreetly. He sanctified it. He built the religious life of Israel around meals. The Passover was a meal — roasted lamb, bitter herbs, unleavened bread, eaten standing and ready to move (Exodus 12). The festivals were feasts. The fellowship offerings ended with the worshippers eating in God's presence. When God wanted to seal the covenant at Sinai, the elders went up the mountain, saw God, "and they ate and drank" (Exodus 24:11). They beheld the glory of God and they had a meal. The two were not in tension. The meal was the communion.

When the Son of God came, he came eating. He ate so much, with such a range of people, that his enemies coined an insult: "a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners" (Matthew 11:19). Read the Gospels watching for tables and you will be startled how much of his ministry happens at them. He is at Levi's table, Zacchaeus's table, the Pharisee's table, the wedding at Cana where he keeps the wine flowing. He feeds five thousand on a hillside because he will not send hungry bodies away. He tells parable after parable about feasts, and he describes the end of all things as a wedding supper. The kingdom of God, in his mouth, tastes like a banquet.

Then, on the last night, when he wanted to give his disciples something to hold onto across the centuries, he did not give them a doctrine to memorize. He gave them a meal. "This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me" (Luke 22:19). He took the most ordinary substances on the table — bread, wine — and made them the means by which his people would commune with him until he returns. He could have asked us to remember him by thinking the right thoughts. He asked us to eat. To put something in our mouths, to chew and swallow, to receive grace through the body's hunger. The Lord's Supper is the gospel made edible. It is grace you can taste.

This tells us something the Greek lie could never accept: that the path to God runs through the body, not around it. We do not commune with Christ by escaping our appetites. We commune with him by bringing our appetite to his table and being fed. Eating, the most material act we perform, is the act he chose to carry his presence. Matter bears spirit. The bread is not in the way of the grace. The bread is how the grace comes.

But there is a shadow over the table, and we should name it honestly. Because food is so tied to desire, it is one of the first places our desire goes wrong. Paul warned of those "whose god is their belly" (Philippians 3:19) — people whose appetites have become their deity, who organize their lives around the next satisfaction. We know this from the inside. Food becomes the thing we run to when we will not run to God. It becomes comfort we cannot get from him, control we cannot find elsewhere, a private kingdom of pleasure or denial. Eating becomes worship of the self. And on the other side, food becomes a torment — a battlefield of shame and restriction, a body starved or punished in pursuit of an image. The same hunger that was meant to teach us dependence on God gets bent into bondage.

The answer the church has too often given is rules. Eat less. Eat clean. Master the body. But the disordering of food is not finally about quantity; it is about worship. James K. A. Smith's point holds here: our appetites are trained by our habits, and what we repeatedly do at the table forms what we love. You will not fix a disordered hunger by trying harder to control it. You fix it the way Jesus fixed it — by putting the right meal at the center. By learning to taste grace at his table until the lesser hungers lose their grip. The cure for the belly that has become a god is not a stricter diet. It is a better feast.

Augustine, in the Confessions, wrote one of the most honest paragraphs ever written about eating — confessing that he could never be sure, in the middle of a meal, where legitimate need for nourishment ended and the slide into mere indulgence began, and that he ate every day in this uncertain country between necessity and pleasure, asking God for mercy at the table. I find that more useful than any rule. He did not pretend to have solved it. He brought his hunger to God daily and asked for grace in it. That is the posture. Not mastery. Mercy.

I think of my own table, with sons around it over the years, and how much of what mattered most happened there — not in the words said but in the fact of the bodies gathered, fed, present, ordinary. A family is held together at a table more than anywhere else. So is a church. So, it turns out, is the whole drama of redemption, which begins in a garden full of fruit and ends at a wedding supper, with a cross-shaped meal in between.

God could have fed us by command. He chose to feed us by bread. Come and eat.
chapters.verdict: God could have fed us by command. He chose to feed us by bread.
reflect: What does your relationship with food reveal about what you actually trust to satisfy you?
When did eating last become worship for you, and when did it last become an idol?
Why do you think Jesus chose a meal, not a lecture, as the way to be remembered?

chapters.title: One Flesh
chapters.summary: Sexuality is not a problem the spirit must overcome but a created good with a created meaning, and the culture and the church have lied about it in opposite directions.
chapters.body:
The church has lied about sex in two directions, and most of us were wounded by one of them before we were old enough to name it.

The first lie is the old dualism wearing a religious robe. It says the body's sexual desire is dirty, that the most spiritual people would be free of it, that sex is a concession God makes to weakness rather than a good he created. Generations of Christians absorbed this and learned to feel that their desire was their shame, that the holiest thing would be to have no body at all. Augustine, for all his genius, carried some of this and passed it down, reading the transmission of sin too tightly through the act of conceiving, leaving the church with centuries of suspicion that sexuality and sanctity were natural enemies.

The second lie is newer and louder. It says the body is a vehicle for pleasure that answers to nothing — that desire is self-justifying, that the only sin is restraint, that what you do with your flesh has no meaning beyond the sensation it produces. This lie also treats the body as separate from the self, just in the opposite way. The old lie said the body does not matter because the soul is what counts. The new lie says the body does not matter because nothing counts but the appetite of the moment. Both detach the body from the person. Both are forms of the same dualism.

Scripture refuses both. Go back to the garden, before anything is broken. "Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh. And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed" (Genesis 2:24-25). One flesh — a phrase that means more than the act, though it includes the act fully. And naked without shame. Before the fall, sexuality is good, bodily, unashamed, and it means something: the joining of two whole persons into a union the Bible treats as nearly mystical. Sex is not the spirit slumming in the flesh. It is the flesh telling the truth about a covenant.

That is the category we have lost: sex as language. The body, in the marital union, says something. It says, with the whole self, *I am wholly given to you and you to me, permanently, without reservation.* That is what the act means. It is a bodily vow. And this is why Paul reacts so violently to the Corinthians sleeping with prostitutes — not out of prudishness, but because the body is speaking. "Do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her?" (1 Corinthians 6:16). You cannot use the body's language of total self-giving to say something your will does not mean. When you do, the body lies. And the lie is not trivial, because it is told with the deepest grammar God gave us.

This is why the biblical sexual ethic, which the world finds absurd, is not arbitrary. It is the insistence that the body's language be kept true — that the vow the body makes in the act be the vow the person actually makes in the covenant. The boundaries are not God hating the body's pleasure. They are God protecting the body's meaning. He made the language. He wants it to tell the truth.

Now I have to be a pastor here and not just a theologian, because this is the territory where people are most wounded and most alone. Most of you reading this carry something — a history, a struggle, a desire that frightens you, a marriage where the language has gone cold, a past where the body said things you wish it had not. The church too often meets all of that with rules and disgust, which is just the old lie again, telling people their bodies are the enemy. That is not the gospel. The gospel says the body is good, the desire is not your shame, and the God who made you a sexual being is not embarrassed by you. He is the one who pronounced it very good.

James K. A. Smith's insight matters here too: our desires are not first chosen but formed, trained by what we repeatedly behold and do. We live in a world engineered to disorder sexual desire — a near-infinite supply of images designed to detach arousal from any person, any covenant, any truth, and to retrain the body to want a lie. You will not master that by willpower in the moment. By the moment it is too late; the desire is already shaped. The reordering of sexual desire is the slow work of being formed by better loves, in real bodies, in real covenant, over real time. It is liturgical before it is volitional.

And we have to say, with the same breath, that the single life is not a lesser life, not a holding pattern for people who have not yet found a body to join to. Jesus was single. Paul was single. The Bible treats celibacy as a genuine and honored way of giving the body to God — not by escaping sexuality but by offering it, by saying with the body, *I am wholly given to the kingdom.* The body still speaks. It just speaks a different true sentence. The married body and the celibate body both bear witness; neither is a defect.

I have counseled couples whose marriages were dying in the bedroom and could not figure out why the rest was dying too, and the connection is not mysterious once you see the body as a language. When the body stops telling the truth of the covenant, the covenant grows cold in every room. And I have sat with people drowning in shame over desires they never asked for, who needed to hear, first, that God made the body good before they could hear anything about how to live in it. The order matters. Goodness first. Always goodness first.

The body is not a vehicle for pleasure or a thing to despise. It is a language. The only question is whether it is telling the truth.
chapters.verdict: The body is not a vehicle for pleasure or a thing to despise. It is a language, and it can tell the truth or lie.
reflect: Where have you absorbed the lie that the body's desires are inherently shameful, and where the lie that they answer to nothing?
What is your sexuality saying, true or false, with the language of your body?
How does the goodness of the body change the way you think about your own desire?

chapters.title: Six Days and a Sabbath
chapters.summary: Work is part of the creation God called good, and rest is a command, not a reward; both are bodily, and a culture that idolizes one and despises the other has misread the goodness of the flesh.
chapters.body:
Before there was any sin in the world, there was work. God put the man in the garden "to work it and keep it" (Genesis 2:15) — not as punishment, because nothing had gone wrong yet, but as vocation. To be human is to have something to do with your hands. The image of God in us includes the impulse to make, to cultivate, to bring order out of raw material, because the God whose image we bear is himself a worker. The first thing the Bible tells us about God is that he labored for six days and made a world.

We have lost this. We tend to think of work as the curse — the thing we do to survive until the weekend, the necessary evil between the parts of life that count. But the curse did not invent work. The curse made work hard. "Cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it... by the sweat of your face you shall eat bread" (Genesis 3:17-19). The thorns came with the fall. The frustration, the futility, the sense that your effort is fighting against the grain of a broken world — that is the curse on work. But the work itself is older than the curse and survives it. Adam tended the garden before there were thorns. You were made to labor with your body, and it was good.

This dignifies the most ordinary work. Eugene Peterson spent his life insisting that there is no division between sacred and secular labor — that a person tending a field or fixing a machine or raising children is doing holy work as surely as a pastor in a pulpit. The hands matter. The body's labor matters. There is no spiritual hierarchy that puts the work of the mind above the work of the hands, or church work above farm work. The Greek lie ranked them — the contemplative life above the active, the cleric above the laborer. The Bible ranks them differently or not at all. Jesus spent the vast majority of his earthly life as a tradesman, working wood with his hands, and God called that hidden bodily labor part of the perfect obedience of his Son.

But here is the other half, and it is the half we are losing fastest. God worked six days and on the seventh he rested, and he commanded his people to do the same — not as a suggestion, not as self-care, but as one of the ten words spoken from the mountain. "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy... in it you shall not do any work" (Exodus 20:8-10). And notice the reason given: "For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth... and rested on the seventh day" (Exodus 20:11). You rest because God rested. The Sabbath is built into the architecture of creation itself.

Sabbath is the most counter-cultural command in the Bible for a people like us, because it strikes directly at the idol of productivity. To stop — fully, for a whole day, to cease from work and from the anxiety of work — is to confess with your body that the world does not depend on you. That God ran the universe before you were born and will run it after you die and can certainly manage one day without your output. The Sabbath is a weekly act of trust enacted in the flesh. You lie down. You stop. You let the fields go untended and the emails unanswered, and the world does not end, and in that not-ending you learn the truth: you were never the one holding it together.

Brueggemann wrote a small, sharp book calling Sabbath an act of resistance against the totalizing demands of an economy that wants every hour, every body, every ounce of attention — a culture he called a system of anxious productivity that can never rest because it is always afraid there will not be enough. Sabbath is the refusal of that anxiety. It declares that there is enough, that God provides, that human worth is not measured in output. To keep Sabbath is to step off the machine and announce that you are not a machine — that you are a creature, beloved, who is allowed to stop.

I have to confess that of everything in this book, this is where I have failed most consistently. A pastor's week has no edges, as I said before, and Sunday — the day I most needed to receive rest — was my hardest working day. For years I told myself the work was too important to stop, which is only ever the idol talking. The work is never important enough to make you God, and that is what refusing to rest finally claims: that you are indispensable, that the kingdom cannot spare you, that you must hold the world together by your sweat. It is exhausting because it is a lie, and the body knows it long before the soul admits it. My body told me the truth for years while my schedule called it weakness.

There is a deeper rest underneath the weekly one. The writer of Hebrews says that all the Sabbaths point to a final rest, that "there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God" (Hebrews 4:9), and that we enter it not by working harder but by ceasing from our works as God did from his. The whole gospel is a Sabbath: stop trying to save yourself, stop the frantic labor of earning, and rest in what Christ has finished. The body that learns to stop one day a week is being trained for the deeper stopping — the laying down of the burden of being your own savior.

God worked, and God rested, and he was not ashamed of either. Neither labor nor rest is beneath him. Stop pretending one of them is beneath you.
chapters.verdict: God worked, and God rested, and he was not ashamed of either.
reflect: Do you treat your work as a calling, a curse, or an identity?
When did you last keep a real Sabbath — a full stop, not a recovery day for more work?
What are you afraid will happen if you stop, and what does that fear reveal about who you think is holding the world together?

chapters.title: The Weight of Suffering
chapters.summary: A theology of the body has to reckon honestly with pain, and the Christian answer is not an explanation but a presence — a God who suffered in a body and does not stand at a distance from ours.
chapters.body:
Any theology of the body that does not deal with pain is a fraud, because the body's most insistent message, across a lifetime, is that it can hurt. We are not discussing an abstraction. Somewhere as you read this, a body is failing. A diagnosis has arrived. A pain that will not name itself or leave. The slow erosion of a faculty once taken for granted. The watching of a body you love break down while you can do nothing. This is the country every human being eventually enters, and a faith that has nothing to say there is no faith worth keeping.

The church has too often said the wrong things. It has offered explanations — God is teaching you something, everything happens for a reason, this is part of a plan you cannot see — and these explanations, even when they contain fragments of truth, land on a suffering body like blows. Job's friends did this. They sat with him in silence for seven days, which was the only wise thing they did, and then they opened their mouths and spent thirty chapters explaining his agony to him, insisting it must be his fault, defending God's justice at the expense of Job's actual suffering. And at the end God turns to them in anger: "You have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7). Job, who shouted and accused and demanded an audience with God, spoke rightly. The friends, who explained, did not. Let that sink into every well-meaning person who has ever tried to make sense of someone else's pain.

Because here is what is striking about the book of Job: God never explains. The whole book builds toward an answer, and when God finally speaks out of the whirlwind, he does not give Job a reason. He gives Job himself — a torrent of questions about the wild goodness of creation, the sea and the storm and the creatures no human controls. And somehow it is enough. Not an explanation, but an encounter. Job says, "I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you" (Job 42:5). The suffering was not explained. It was inhabited by the presence of God.

This is the deepest thing the gospel has to say about pain, and it is not a theory. It is a body on a cross. The God of the Bible does not stand outside human suffering, issuing reasons from a safe distance. He entered it. He took a body precisely so that he could suffer in it — and not gently. Isaiah saw it centuries before: "a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief... he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows" (Isaiah 53:3-4). In Gethsemane he sweat and shook and begged for the cup to pass. On the cross he was scourged, pierced, suffocated, and he cried out the opening line of a psalm of utter abandonment: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46). God in a body, screaming the question every sufferer screams. He did not answer the question from above. He came down and asked it from inside.

Bonhoeffer, writing from a Nazi prison cell before they hanged him, came to a conclusion that has held me through more bedsides than I can count: that only a suffering God can help. The God of the philosophers, untouched and untouchable, is no use to a person in agony. But the God of the cross is God allowing himself to be pushed out of the world and onto a gibbet — weak, suffering, present in the pain rather than absent above it. Bonhoeffer wrote that the Bible directs us not to a God of power who removes our suffering but to a God who suffers with us. That is not a smaller comfort. It is the only comfort that survives contact with real pain.

So what do we have to offer the suffering body? Not an explanation. We have a presence — God's, and ours in his name. The most Christlike thing you can do for a person whose body is breaking is what Job's friends did before they ruined it: come, and sit, and stay, and shut up. Be a body present to a suffering body. Do not explain. Do not fix. Do not hand them a reason that costs you nothing and costs them their last comfort. Just be there, flesh beside flesh, the way God came to be flesh beside our flesh. Incarnation is the model for the sickroom. You show up in your body because that is how God showed up for us.

I will not pretend I have always done this well. I have been the friend who explained. I have stood at a bedside afraid of the silence and filled it with words because the words protected me from the helplessness. I have offered reasons that I now know wounded people I loved. The longer I pastor, the less I say in those rooms and the longer I stay. I have learned that my body present and quiet preaches more of the gospel than my best paragraph about the sovereignty of God. The sufferer does not need my theology of pain. They need a face that will not leave.

And I will not pretend the presence makes the pain acceptable. It does not. Suffering is an enemy, not a friend — the Bible calls death the last enemy, and it does not negotiate with it. We are not asked to like it or to call it good. We are asked to bring it, raw, to a God who has felt it, and to refuse the lie that he is far off. Lament is faith with its body still hurting. The psalms are full of it. "How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?" (Psalm 13:1). That is in the Bible. God put the scream in his own songbook.

God did not answer suffering with a reason. He answered it with a body. When you have nothing to say, bring yours.
chapters.verdict: God did not answer suffering with a reason. He answered it with a body.
reflect: What suffering in your body or someone you love's body has made God feel distant or cruel?
Have you been offered explanations for pain that wounded you further, and what would presence have looked like instead?
How does the suffering of Jesus in his own body change what you can bring to God?

chapters.title: The Body That Ages
chapters.summary: Aging is not a malfunction to be cured but a creaturely reality the Bible treats with honor, and a culture terrified of growing old has lost the wisdom that comes only through the body's decline.
chapters.body:
We live among people terrified of growing old, and we have built an entire economy on the terror. Billions of dollars move every year on the promise of reversing what cannot be reversed — the lines, the gray, the slowing, the softening. Aging has been reclassified from a stage of life into a disease to be treated, a failure of self-management, a thing to be hidden and apologized for. We do not honor the old. We pity them, or we ignore them, or we warehouse them out of sight. And underneath it all is the oldest lie in this book wearing yet another mask: that the body is the real problem, and the body's decline is the deepest threat to who we are.

The Bible does not flinch from the reality of aging. It is honest — brutally so. Read the end of Ecclesiastes, where the Preacher describes old age as a house falling into disrepair: "the keepers of the house tremble, and the strong men are bent, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those who look through the windows are dimmed" (Ecclesiastes 12:3). The hands shake, the legs weaken, the teeth go, the eyes dim. The body fails. Scripture does not pretend otherwise; it does not sell you a cream. "Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come" (Ecclesiastes 12:1). The days are coming for all of us, and they are hard.

But — and here is the turn the world cannot make — the Bible treats the aging body with honor rather than horror. "Gray hair is a crown of glory; it is gained in a righteous life" (Proverbs 16:31). A crown. The very thing we spend money to hide, Scripture calls a crown. "Stand up in the presence of the aged, show respect for the elderly" (Leviticus 19:32). The fading body is not a thing to be embarrassed by. It is a thing to be honored, because it carries something the young body does not have: the weight of years, the wisdom that comes only through time, the testimony of a life that has lasted.

And there is something the failing body teaches that the strong body cannot. The strong body lies to us. It tells us we are self-sufficient, durable, in control — it lets us maintain the illusion of being our own god, because it does what we ask and does not yet betray us. The aging body strips that illusion away. It teaches us, slowly and undeniably, that we are creatures: dependent, finite, mortal, held by something other than our own strength. This is not cruelty. It is grace, though it does not feel like it. Paul names the rhythm exactly: "Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day" (2 Corinthians 4:16). The outer wasting and the inner renewing happen at the same time, in the same person, and the one is somehow the soil of the other. The body's decline can become the place where the soul finally grows up.

This is why a culture that despises the old loses more than it knows. It loses the wisdom that only the aged body carries. It loses the witness of people who have lived long enough to know what matters and what does not. The young chase what the old have already learned cannot satisfy. We have severed the generations — separated the old from the young, the dying from the living, so that most people now reach middle age without ever having sat with someone in their final years and learned what a human face looks like at the end. We have made aging invisible, and in doing so we have made ourselves stupid about the one thing that is certainly coming for us all.

I have spent a great deal of my ministry with the old, and I want to tell you what their bodies have taught me, because it is the opposite of what the culture says. I have watched people lose nearly everything the world counts as worth — strength, beauty, independence, the ability to do — and grow more luminous as they lost it. I have held the hand of someone who could no longer feed herself and felt, unmistakably, that I was in the presence of more soul, not less. The fading of the body did not diminish the person. It concentrated them. Like a fire burning down to its hottest coals. The dross went and the gold stayed, and the gold was brighter for the burning.

I am not yet old, and I write this with the appropriate fear of a man who has not yet walked through what he is describing. But I have decided what I want to believe when my own body begins its decline, and I am trying to believe it now so that it is already settled when the days come. I want to refuse the lie that my worth declines with my strength. I want to receive the failing of the body not as the theft of my dignity but as the place God means to finish a work he started — sanding down the self-sufficiency I clung to in my strong years, teaching me at last to be wholly dependent, which is what a creature was always supposed to be.

Because the deepest thing about aging is what it points toward. Every wrinkle, every weakening, every reminder that the body is temporary is a finger pointing past itself toward the resurrection. The body wears out precisely so that we will stop trusting it to save us and start longing for the body God has promised. We will get to that promise in the end. For now it is enough to say: the decline is not the end of the story, and it is not the loss of who you are.

The fading body is not the loss of your dignity. In Scripture it is the gathering of it. Honor the old. You are becoming them.
chapters.verdict: The fading body is not the loss of your dignity. In Scripture it is the gathering of it.
reflect: What do you fear most about growing old, and where did you learn to fear it?
Whose aging or dying have you witnessed up close, and what did their body teach you?
How would you live differently if you believed your worth did not decline with your strength?

chapters.title: The Redemption of Our Bodies
chapters.summary: The Christian hope is not the soul escaping to heaven but the resurrection of the body and the renewal of all creation; everything in this book finds its end here, at the empty tomb and the new earth.
chapters.body:
We come to the end, and the end is where the whole argument of this book either stands or falls. Because if the Christian hope is finally that the soul escapes the body and floats off to a disembodied heaven, then everything I have written is wrong, and the Greek lie wins in the last chapter. But it is not. The Christian hope, from beginning to end, is the resurrection of the body and the renewal of all creation. God's purpose was never to save us *from* the material world. It was to redeem it.

Start where the church has always started: the empty tomb. When the women came to the grave on the third day, it was not Jesus's soul that had gone to heaven while his corpse stayed behind. The body was gone. The grave was empty. And when he appeared to the disciples, he was emphatic about what he was. "See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have" (Luke 24:39). He showed them the wounds. He ate a piece of broiled fish in front of them to prove he was not a ghost (Luke 24:42-43). The resurrected Christ is not less physical than before. He is more — a body so real it could be touched, so transformed it could pass through doors. This is the firstfruits of what is promised to us.

N. T. Wright has spent much of his life trying to wake the church from a sub-Christian hope, arguing that "heaven" as most people imagine it — a disembodied, ethereal forever — is not the biblical end at all. The Bible's hope is life after life after death: first a temporary rest with Christ, and then, at the last day, resurrection — new bodies in a new creation, heaven and earth joined. Wright calls the popular escape-to-the-clouds picture a distortion that has eaten the church's hope from the inside. The point of the gospel is not that we go up to heaven when we die. It is that heaven comes down, that God remakes the world, and that we are raised in bodies to live in it. The whole sweep of his work, especially *Surprised by Hope*, is a recovery of this: bodily resurrection, not spiritual escape.

Paul lays it out in the great resurrection chapter. He knows the objection — "How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?" (1 Corinthians 15:35) — and he answers with the image of a seed. "What you sow does not come to life unless it dies... It is sown a perishable body; it is raised imperishable... It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body" (1 Corinthians 15:36, 42-44). Do not misread "spiritual body." Paul does not mean a ghostly, non-physical body; that would be a contradiction in his vocabulary. He means a body animated and ruled by the Spirit, a body no longer subject to decay — the same continuity as a seed and the plant that rises from it, recognizably connected and gloriously transformed. The body that is raised is *your* body, redeemed, not a replacement issued because the first one was a mistake.

And it is not just our bodies. Paul's vision is cosmic. "The creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God" (Romans 8:21). The whole groaning creation — the same material world God called very good in the beginning — is going to be liberated, not discarded. And in the same passage Paul names the specific object of our hope: "we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies" (Romans 8:23). The redemption of our bodies. Not the deletion of them. The redemption of them. That phrase is the whole book in three words.

This is where it all lands. Irenaeus said the glory of God is a living human being. The resurrection is that sentence written across eternity — humanity fully alive, in bodies, forever, in a world made new. John's vision at the end of the Bible is not of souls escaping earth but of "the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God" (Revelation 21:2). God comes down. He moves in, again, permanently. "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them" (Revelation 21:3). And he wipes away tears from eyes — actual eyes, in actual faces — because there will still be faces. The end of the story is not less physical than the beginning. It is the beginning healed.

So consider what this does to everything we have walked through. If the body is going to be raised, then what you do with your body now matters eternally, because this body and that one are the same seed and plant. The hunger you bring to the table, the rest you take or refuse, the way your sexuality tells the truth or lies, the suffering you endure, the aging you fear — none of it is a holding pattern for a soul waiting to escape. It is the early chapters of a body God intends to raise. Your present flesh is not disposable packaging. It is the seed of glory.

I came to faith out of atheism expecting a religion of escape, and I have spent these pages telling you it is the opposite. I want to end with the cost of that, because Bell's endings do not resolve, and this one should not either. The resurrection hope does not make the present body easy. You will still age. You will still suffer. The body you are in will still go into the ground, and the people you love will go before you, and you will stand at gravesides where the promise feels thin against the weight of the dirt. The hope does not spare you that. It only refuses to let the grave have the last word.

Because the grave does not have the last word. It had Jesus for three days and then it was empty, and the women ran from it in fear and joy, and the world has never been the same. God's last word over your body is not the grave. It is resurrection. Carry that out into your Tuesday, and into your aging, and into the room where someone you love is dying. The Word became flesh, and the flesh was raised, and so will yours be.

This is the faith. It was always about the body. It always will be.
chapters.verdict: God's last word over your body is not the grave. It is resurrection.
reflect: Have you been hoping for the wrong heaven — a disembodied escape rather than the resurrection of the body?
How does the promise of a redeemed body change the way you treat your present one?
What in you still secretly wants to be rid of the body rather than to see it raised?
